title: Reading a bank statement
examples: How do I tell if a charge is a debit or a credit?
What is a typical bank fee I should watch out for?
If I see a charge I don't recognize, what should I do?

explain.say: Today we are learning to read a bank statement carefully.
A debit means money is leaving your account.
A credit means money is being added to your account.
Fees are charges for services your bank provides.

items: Overdraft Fee: Using too much money
ATM Fee: Using another bank's machine
Monthly Service Fee: Keeping the account open

explain.say: Look at your statement to see the flow of money.
In real life, paying for online shopping shows these concepts.

faq.q: What is the difference between a debit and a withdrawal?
faq.a: A withdrawal is a specific type of debit. It means you are physically taking cash out of an ATM or bank teller.
asks: Is a withdrawal always a debit?
What is the difference between debit and cash taken?

faq.q: If I see a charge I don't recognize, what should I do?
faq.a: First, check the date and amount against your records. If it is still unknown, contact your bank immediately to report potential fraud.
asks: Who do I call about a strange charge?
What is the first step for an unknown transaction?

faq.q: Are fees always bad things to see on my statement?
faq.a: Not always; some fees are unavoidable for certain services. However, you should always check the bank's fee schedule to avoid surprise charges.
asks: Can I avoid all bank fees?
What are common types of bank fees?

faq.q: Do credits always mean I received money?
faq.a: Credits usually mean money is added, but sometimes it can be a bank correction or an interest payment, which is still money coming in.
asks: Can a credit be something else?
What is interest shown as on a statement?

faq.q: How often should I check my bank statement?
faq.a: It is best practice to check your statement regularly, perhaps weekly, to catch any unauthorized transactions quickly.
asks: How often should I monitor my account?
What is the best monitoring frequency?

facts: Debits reduce the money available in your account.
Credits increase the money available in your account.
Bank fees are charges for services provided by the financial institution.
Always compare the transaction date with when you actually made the purchase.

quiz.say: A deposit of your paycheck shows up on the statement. Is this a debit or a credit?
quiz.why: A deposit adds money to your account, which is the definition of a credit.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because the statement must show a clear direction for the money movement.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because a debit means money is leaving your account, not entering it.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because a fee is a charge, which would be a debit, not the deposit itself.

quiz.say: You use an ATM at a different bank. The charge listed is for the service. What is this charge?
quiz.why: The charge for using an external machine is a specific service fee.

wrong.0: This is too general; 'Fee' tells you the reason for the debit.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because the charge is money leaving your account, not money coming in.
wrong.3: While it reduces your balance, 'Fee' is the specific classification for this type of charge.

quiz.say: If your account balance was one hundred dollars, and you bought coffee for five dollars, what is the resulting change?
quiz.why: Buying something causes money to leave your account, which is recorded as a debit.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because while it is a fee, the general term for spending money is debit.
wrong.1: This is incorrect because spending money always reduces the available balance.
wrong.3: This is incorrect because a credit would mean you received five extra dollars.
